newsitem.title: USA: Canadians re-open largest gold mines in Kazakstan.
newsitem.headline: Canadians re-open largest gold mines in Kazakstan.

text.p: A new Canadian public company, has succeeded in re-opening the largest gold mines in Kazakhstan, with the first exports of gold expected next month, and it has an option to buy the 3.1 million ounces of gold reserves for only US$20 million.

"Larger mining companies may not have been interested in the old state-owned mines, with their debt and labor problems, but we were already on the ground and have dealt with all the local issues successfully," Toronto-based Kazakstan Goldfields Corp chairman Tom Griffis said in an interview. "We're on track to raise production from around 8,000 ounces a month to around 225,000 ounces annually in the next year or two," he said.

Under a management contract awarded in March 1996, Toronto-based Kazakstan Goldfields Corp (KGC) now operates the Kazakhstan state-owned enterprise, Kazakhaltyn, which owns three mines that have produced over 10 million ounces of gold and has remaining resources of over three million ounces.

"But we have an option to purchase the shares in Kazakhaltyn with a strike price of $20 million and we have already invested $14 million in the operation which counts towards the purchase price," Griffis said.

Kazakhstan, is the tenth largest country in the world, extending from the Caspian Sea in the west to China in the east, and is regarded by many industry analysts as the most mineral-rich of the former USSR republics.
But production at the Kazaltyn mines ground to a halt due to financial and technical problems in the wake of the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991.

"Over the past 11 months our team of Canadian mining experts, who have had experience in Asia and Latin America, did due diligence on the Kazakhaltyn mines, reduced staff from 7,000 to 2,500, paid off or came to an arrangement on most debt and put all three mines back into business," KGC president Charles Pitcher said.
"Within the next three to six months our cost per ounce will be below US$250 per ounce," he said.
Start up operations began in September 1996, with about 3,000 ounces produced, which should be up to 12,000 ounces per month in early 1997, Pitcher said.

In addition, the company has an exploration licence covering two blocks totalling three million acres, adjacent to the world-class Vasilkovskoye gold desposit, which could double the current reserve of 3 million ounces.
KGC has been quoted on the Canadian Dealing Network under the trading symbol "KGFC" since October 11, 1996.
KGC's assets in Kazakstan are held through its 75 percent interest in the Gold Pool Joint Venture, with the remaining 25 percent owned by Central Asia Goldfields Corp.
In turn, Central Asia Goldfields owns 22 percent of KGC.
The Gold Pool Joint Venture is the Kazakstan-based legal entity which owns the management contract and the rights to acquire the mines and reserves.
Central Asia is a gold exploration company which has a portfolio of properties in Kazakstan in joint venture with Kazakstan private companies.
KGC currently has cash reserves of US$7 million, no debt, smelter and union contracts in place in Kazakstan, and a recently secured gold export licence.
KGC has been trading around C$1.20 per share with about 40 million shares fully diluted, and cash flow per share potential of about 40 cents per share in 1997, Griffis said.
"We have already had expressions of interest in Kazakstan Goldfields from several large investors and we may seek a stock exchange listing soon," Griffis said.
